title: “That was the catalyst for everything that happened next”: A qualitative exploration of the turning points that lead to mental health recovery
description:
Introduction: Whilst mental health recovery is well studied through interviews and qualitative analyses, little information is available on how the processes unfold to catalyse change at specific points over the life course.  This study aims to explore the experiences of turning points that facilitate recovery and the internal and external factors that enable these experiences of change.
Methods: This study used life course approaches and semi-structured interviews to explore people’s experiences of turning points towards recovery. Twelve participants with a history of recovery from mental health challenges were recruited via social media and posters displayed in the community. Reflexive thematic analysis was used to analyse the data.
Results: Five main themes were identified, which were delineated into external and internal recovery processes. The external processes were Contextual Influences and Interpersonal Dynamics. The internal processes were Agency and Ownership, Transformative Insights, and Healing from Within.
Conclusion: The findings were consistent with the wider literature. Clinical implications of the research include creating environmental contexts that facilitate recovery, offering community-focused approaches to mental health care, and involving stakeholders in service development and provision.

title: Chunking improves working memory via compression, not direct retrieval from long-term memory
description: Working memory (WM) capacity is severely limited. Chunking, the process of grouping related items in WM, circumvents this limit and drastically improves performance. Despite decades of research, the mechanism underlying this benefit remains debated. One account proposes that statistical regularities allow multiple items to be compressed into structured WM representations, whereas another argues that structured associations are stored in long‑term memory (LTM) and reinstated at recall, effectively offloading storage demands. These accounts imply fundamentally different interactions between WM and long-term knowledge, yet in most paradigms, they make indistinguishable behavioural predictions. Here, we dissociate them by introducing small, continuous trial‑to‑trial variations in the hues of learned colour pairs, allowing us to test whether chunking benefits arise from compressed memory for the current hue (WM) or retrieval of long‑run feature means (LTM). Across two delayed colour report experiments, chunking reliably improved recall relative to unchunkable arrays. Participants remained sensitive to trial‑specific feature variations, indicating that responses were not driven by retrieval of feature means from LTM templates. At the same time, responses were systematically biased toward each item’s long‑run mean, especially on chunkable trials. To explain this bias, we fit psychophysical models derived from the competing compression and LTM‑retrieval accounts. The compression-based model, in which compression produces graded biases toward learned means within WM, outperformed the LTM-retrieval and baseline models. In a second experiment, we examined whether these biases arise during encoding/maintenance or at the recall stage. Cues in the maintenance period indicating which item would be probed improved recall accuracy but did not reduce bias toward learned structure, indicating that the bias arose during encoding or early maintenance rather than retrieval. title: Olfactory Disgust Conditioning across Multiple Response Systems: The Role of Temporal Contiguity
description: Disgust plays an important role in the development and maintenance of various mental disorders, with Pavlovian conditioning proposed as a potential underlying mechanism. Yet, psychophysiological correlates of disgust conditioning remain poorly understood, especially in olfactory conditioning, despite the notion that odors may be particularly effective in eliciting disgust. Disgust acquisition has also been theorized to rely comparatively less on the temporal contiguity between conditioned (CS) and unconditioned stimuli (UCS) (i.e., trace vs. delay conditioning), but there is little evidence to support this assumption. Based on a comprehensive assessment of self-report measures (valence, disgust, arousal, and expectancy ratings) and psychophysiological markers (respiratory latency [RSP], heart-period [HP] modulation, skin conductance response [SCR], and pupil dilation response [PDR]) in different response windows, the present study aimed to advance the understanding of disgust conditioning and to examine whether the degree of temporal contiguity of CS and UCS modulates conditioned responses. A total of 71 participants (54 women) underwent a within-subjects design consisting of two conditioning sessions with faces as CS and individualized aversive odors as UCS. Between sessions, the temporal contiguity of CS and UCS (delay conditioning: 2s overlap between CS and UCS; trace conditioning: 4s gap interval between CS offset and UCS onset) was varied. Evidence for differential conditioning (CS+ vs. CS-) was found across all self-report and most psychophysiological measures in both CS- and UCS-locked response windows. Trace conditioning was associated with attenuated responding but not reduced response differentiation in HP modulation, SCR, and PDR (both windows), with an interaction emerging only for RSP (CS-locked window). Controlling for trial-by-trial changes in RSP did not abolish previously identified conditioning effects, despite significant modulation of HP by RSP.

title: The zebrafish alarm response as embodied semiosis: An approach between enactivism and biosemiotics
description: Mechanistic approaches in behavioral neuroscience often overlook the situated, embodied, and meaning‑generating dimensions of animal behavior. This paper builds a theoretical bridge between enactivism and biosemiotics – two frameworks that place sense‑making at the core of life – and grounds the synthesis in an empirical case: the alarm reaction of zebrafish (Danio rerio). The conspecific alarm substance (CAS) is not merely a chemical trigger but a semiotic sign that acquires meaning through the fish’s sensorimotor engagement with its ecological and social context. Using Peircean concepts, we analyze how the sign‑vehicle (the CAS mixture), its dynamic object (predation risk), and its interpretants (defensive actions, physiological changes) are enacted across multiple scales: from an individual’s sensorimotor loops to the emergent, collective interpretation of a shoal. This “embodied semiosis” perspective reveals that meaning is not pre‑given but constituted through the animal’s active, value‑laden interaction with its Umwelt. By integrating semiopsychology, which operationalizes semiotic categories for empirical inquiry, with enactivism’s emphasis on embodiment and agency, the framework yields testable predictions about how social coupling, context, and allostatic regulation shape alarm responses. We discuss operational challenges and the risk of overgeneralizing collective interpretants, while arguing that the approach offers a fertile alternative to representationalist accounts of adaptive behavior. Embodied semiosis thus provides a common language for studying how organisms, from zebrafish to humans, enact significance through their living, sense‑making bodies.

title: GenAI as Complete Cognitive Automation for Untrained Users at Population Scale: Implications for Human Factors and Ergonomics
description: Generative AI (GenAI) systems provide complete cognitive task outputs to untrained users across unrestricted domains at population scale, creating an unprecedented form of automation. We apply Parasuraman et al.’s (2000) framework of four cognitive automation stages to characterize this shift. GenAI automates all four stages simultaneously: information acquisition, information analysis, decision selection, and action specification. Classical automation effects (e.g., the “lumberjack effect”) were established exclusively in trained operators working within bounded domains. Whether these effects persist, intensify, or transform when GenAI violates all previous scope conditions simultaneously remains an open empirical question. Nearly a billion people now use this technology without the empirical foundation needed to predict human performance consequences. This commentary maps how GenAI’s deployment configuration exceeds automation theory’s empirical boundaries and identifies critical research questions to guide investigation of human performance and safety in this understudied area of automation design.

title: Behavioral goal-setting for veterans with trauma distress: A qualitative report of goals and outcomes in a self-guided intervention
description: Goal setting is a key component to psychotherapy; however, little is known about self-generated goals of veterans with trauma distress. In this study, we explored goals set by veterans within a positive psychology intervention. Qualitative data were collected in an web-based intervention study that targeted positive social processes by eliciting moral elevation—feeling inspired by others’ virtuous actions. The sample included veterans who endorsed significant PTSD symptoms and moral injury distress. Participants completed 8 web-based, self-guided sessions that included setting their own goals and reporting on the outcomes in subsequent sessions using text responses. All qualitative data were coded using an inductive approach by study personnel. Separate raters reviewed all codes independently to identify themes. The most common themes of self-generated goals included prosocial behavior, enhancing family relationships, and self-improvement activities. Themes for successful outcome reactions included positive emotions and noticing a positive impact on others. Common themes for barriers included other responsibilities, interfering negative emotions, lack of motivation, and personal limitations. Strategies to overcome barriers were also identified. These qualitative findings offer a novel contribution by providing greater context for behavioral goal pursuits among veterans with trauma distress and warrant further examination into the goal setting process for this population.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Precision Brain Stimulation: From Neuroimaging to Foundation Models and Virtual Brains
description: Precision brain stimulation is an emerging paradigm in clinical neuroscience, offering the potential to modulate dysfunctional circuits with individualized protocols for disorders ranging from neurological to psychiatric disorders. The convergence of large-scale neuroimaging datasets, physics-based computational models, and artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly accelerating this vision. This review integrates developments across four domains. First, we examine the availability and harmonisation of population-level neuroimaging repositories such as the UK Biobank, Human Connectome Project (HCP), Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study, and ENIGMA consortium, which provide unprecedented insight into structural and functional variability relevant to stimulation targeting biomarkers. Second, we trace the evolution of physics-based and computational head models that simulate electric, magnetic, and acoustic field distributions across non-invasive modalities—including transcranial electrical stimulation (tES), temporal interference stimulation (TIS), transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), and transcranial focused ultrasound (tFUS)—as well as invasive techniques such as cortical and deep brain stimulation. Third, we highlight the emergence of AI-driven brain imaging foundation models, such as NeuroSTORM, which leverage large-scale pre-training to enable predictive modeling of brain states, treatment response, and individualized stimulation optimization. Fourth, we present the concept of individualized digital twin brains—computational avatars that integrate neuroimaging, physics-based simulations, and AI foundation models to simulate and test stimulation strategies tailored to each patient’s connectivity and activation profile. Finally, we illustrate translational potential through two clinical use-case scenarios: precision targeting for seizure suppression in epilepsy and individualized stimulation for craving reduction and relapse prevention in addiction.

title: Cognitive-Computational Phenotyping of  Anxiety and Anhedonia
description: Internalising psychopathology has been associated with deficits in various cognitive tasks. However, it remains unclear whether these tasks capture distinct aspects of psychopathology and whether combining multiple tasks adds value. This study tested which parameters from four established cognitive tasks were specifically associated with anxiety/depression or anhedonia/apathy and assessed multivariate patterns across tasks. Two online samples (n=359, n=588), pre-screened to maximise variance in anxiety and anhedonia, completed all tasks. Anhedonia/apathy was associated with better reinforcement learning and increased foraging versus hiding, whereas anxiety/depression was associated with impaired reinforcement learning and deficient emotional processing. Parameters from three cognitive tasks predicted the relative severity of anxiety/depression versus anhedonia/apathy symptoms, significantly better than demographics alone but with a small effect size. These findings advance our understanding of the cognitive-computational basis of anhedonia and anxiety and highlight the value of transdiagnostic symptom dimensions.

title: Preschoolers can coordinate with each other to communicate about novel referents
description: Learning language requires learning not only the content of language, but also how to use language to communicate. Iterated reference games provide a window into such skills, requiring rich communication as participants converge on mutually understandable names for initially novel referents. Some early experiments are interpreted as evidence that 4-5-year-old children cannot converge on the mutually understandable names needed to succeed in an iterated reference game. Here, we revisit young children's referential communicative abilities using a simpler, child-friendly version of the iterated reference game paradigm. Across 3 experiments and 82 pairs of children (N=158), we found that 4-5-year-olds could successfully establish reference with each other. Children were 81% accurate, and they often used descriptions similar to their partner's. These findings suggest that children’s capacity to construct effective referring expressions in novel contexts emerges earlier than previously thought, consistent with the view that children show early pragmatic competence in supportive contexts.

title: Characterizing the frequency and content of speech from other children in daylong recordings of infants’ input
description: Infant’s language development is inherently tied to their linguistic input, but the majority of research investigating infant’s input has focused on adult caregiver speech.  However, children do not exclusively interact with adults. In the US, 80% of children’s households include additional children. The focus on adult caregiver input thus does not fully capture the experience of the majority of children.  We quantify infant’s experiences with speech from children, measuring its frequency and content. We find that speech from children is a common feature of the input for infants with older siblings, occurring once every minute. Analyses of content find that children produce the same words more often (lower type-token ratio) and shorter utterances overall, and that their speech contains earlier learned words and more nouns. Speech from children however does not vary from speech from adults in average word frequency or in iconicity. We highlight the importance of considering speech from children for infants with older siblings in our theories of language development.

title: Representational Idiosyncrasy of Psychopathology Across Text Embedding Models: Implications and Practical Suggestions for Clinical Psychological Science
description: The integration of large language models (LLMs) into clinical psychological science has outpaced our understanding of how psychopathology is represented across the diverse model landscape. We analyzed how 21 text embedding models represented 405 items from the HiTOP-SR, a non-public psychopathology measure absent from training data. Exploratory factor analysis of item-level representations at global and domain-specific levels revealed variable structural consistency across models. Globally, structural congruence frequently fell below meaningful thresholds (CC < .85), although broad two-factor solutions showed strong cross-model convergence. Domain-specific congruence varied considerably, with some domains (e.g., Anankastia) showing strong convergence and others (e.g., Antagonism) showing weak convergence. These findings demonstrate that text embedding models may lack a shared representational framework for psychopathology, yielding structures that are idiosyncratic and sensitive to model-specific features and methodological choices. These inconsistencies underscore the need for careful model selection and rigorous evaluation of LLM-based tools.

title: Aquahenosis: A non-pharmacological altered state of consciousness induced by Floatation-REST in individuals with anxiety and depression
description: Floatation-REST (Reduced Environmental Stimulation Therapy) systematically alters sensory and bodily input by combining neutral buoyancy, thermal and proprioceptive neutrality, attenuation of exteroceptive stimulation, and enhancement of cardiorespiratory signaling to the brain. Here we examined whether this non-pharmacological sensory perturbation induces altered states of consciousness and whether specific experiential dimensions are statistically related to changes in affect. In a secondary analysis of a randomized controlled feasibility trial, 75 treatment-seeking adults with anxiety and depression were assigned to six sessions of Floatation-REST with prescribed scheduling, Floatation-REST with preferred scheduling and duration, or a zero-gravity chair comparison condition. Altered states of consciousness were assessed using the 5-Dimensional Altered States of Consciousness Rating Scale, alongside measures of interoceptive awareness and affect. Compared to the chair condition, Floatation-REST was associated with increased interoceptive awareness of cardiorespiratory sensations and an altered state of consciousness characterized by Oceanic Boundlessness, Disembodiment, and Experience of Unity—a pattern we refer to as "aquahenosis." Effects were strongest among participants who selected longer and more flexible float sessions. Experiential profiles selectively overlapped with those reported for psilocybin and ketamine along boundary-dissolution dimensions. These findings identify Floatation-REST as a tractable, non-pharmacological method for inducing specific altered states of consciousness and highlight oceanic boundlessness as an important mediator of the float-induced changes in positive affect.

title: Social Influence in Donation Behavior: The Effect of Mean, Variance, and Psychopathy
description: Charitable giving is a cornerstone of social welfare, and others’ donations can promote individual giving. However, the computational mechanisms through which social information shapes donation behavior, and how individuals differ in their responsiveness, remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated how the statistical properties of others’ donations shape individual giving, and how this was affected by individual differences in socio-affective traits. Across 4 pre-registered experiments (total N = 1,491), participants made donations before and after observing sequential donations from diverse others whose mean and variability were systematically manipulated. We found that observing generous average donations robustly increased individual giving, while observing stingy donations decreased it. Moreover, the variance in social information did not modulate this shift. In parallel, exposure to others’ donations consistently reduced the variability of individual donations, with stronger reductions when others’ donations were more consistent (versus more variable). Computational modeling revealed that a hybrid reinforcement learning model integrating initial donations with learned predictions of others’ donations captured participants’ donation behaviors well. At the individual level, changes in donations following social exposure were consistently positively associated with psychopathic traits. Model-derived parameters further revealed that people with higher psychopathic traits were more susceptible to social information, assigning greater weight to observed donations when making their second decisions. These results were replicated across all experiments, despite variations in donation magnitudes, population type, variability discrepancy, and incentive structures. Together, our findings demonstrate that the statistical structure of social information - its magnitude and variability - shapes the corresponding features of individual donations, and identify psychopathy

title: Beyond Right and Wrong: Evaluating Second-order Social Reasoning in Large Language Models
description: Previous AI alignment efforts have focused primarily on first-order social norms -- teaching models what is socially acceptable or unacceptable (e.g., "do not steal"). However, social intelligence depends not only on norm recognition, but also on anticipating who will enforce it and how (e.g., public shame or even imprisonment).  These second-order expectations, known as metanorms, govern how people respond when social rules are broken.  We introduce a novel framework for evaluating metanorm reasoning in Large Language Models (LLMs) along two dimensions: emotional appraisal and behavioral response, and propose new classification tasks, namely, predicting self-regulation in violators, and other-regulation in observers. We release a multi-perspective dataset, NormReact, of 450 norm violation scenarios, hand-annotated for emotions and behavioral responses across norm violators' gender and observers' social closeness. Current LLMs portray a harsher social world: across six models, they overpredict negative sanctions where humans would expect inaction, and alignment with human judgments deteriorates as social distance increases. These findings suggest that AI systems in norm-sensitive domains, from conflict mediation to policy simulation, may risk producing a distorted picture of social regulation: one that over-represents punishment and under-represents the tolerance, restraint, and relational calibration that characterize actual norm enforcement in the real world.

title: Can we Automate Social Science Concept Harmonization? A Fine-Grained Review of Performance and Failure Modes
description: Conceptual ambiguity is a persistent obstacle to cumulative social science: the same construct appears under different labels, while a single label can stand for distinct constructs. Text-embedding methods offer a scalable route to harmonization, but their value depends on recovering conceptual overlap rather than surface-level lexical similarity. We evaluate 12 pipelines that combine four embedding models with three techniques, calibrated on the European Language Social Science Thesaurus and tested on the APA Thesaurus. Beyond accuracy, five diagnostic tests examine lexical traps, semantic decay, stability, rare-word bias, and alignment with expert taxonomic structure. Harmonization identifies many synonymous labels, but accuracy is uneven and depends on surface form, with errors concentrated in cases central to theory development: low-overlap synonyms, rare terms, and subtle taxonomic distinctions. The diagnostic tests make these successes and failures transparent, giving researchers a reproducible basis for deciding when to trust embedding-based harmonization and when to defer to experts.

title: Between the Steeple and the Golden Stool: Navigating Cultural Conflict, Pentecostal Competition, and the Organisational Resilience Paradox in Asante Baptist Ministry
description:
Background: The intersection of Asante cosmological traditions and Christian ministry constitutes a profoundly contested space in West African Christianity. Despite severe implications for denominational attrition amid aggressive Pentecostal competition, empirical examination of this culture-faith nexus remains sparse. This pioneering study investigates the prevalence, character, and congregational consequences of conflicts between traditional Asante practices and Baptist theology in urban Ghana.
Methods: Employing a robust cross-sectional mixed-methods design, we surveyed 200 ordained Ghana Baptist Convention pastors in the Kumasi Metropolis. Quantitative data underwent rigorous statistical evaluation using Python 3.12, including chi-square tests of independence and Spearman’s rank-order correlation, triangulated with keyword-based thematic analysis of qualitative pastoral narratives.
Results: Findings reveal that 70.5% of pastors consistently navigate culture-faith conflicts, predominantly driven by deeply entrenched taboos (18.0%), bride-price demands (17.0%), and ancestral worship (15.0%). Notably, while 23.0% of pastors reported direct membership attrition to culturally accommodating Pentecostal alternatives, chi-square analysis established no significant statistical association between conflict frequency and attrition (χ² = 6.888, p = 0.549). Spearman correlations demonstrated that pastoral challenge domains operate independently of one another (|ρ|≤0.133). Crucially, the data expose a novel "organisational resilience paradox": despite experiencing profound cultural friction, intense Pentecostal competition, and compounding youth apathy (68.0%), 88.5% of pastors report high congregational effectiveness in community impact.

title: Styles That Heal or Harm: Rethinking Leadership Through the Lens of Employee Well-Being
description:
Introduction: Employee well-being (EWB) is a construct having multiple dimensions that consist of physical, psychological, environmental, and social dimensions. It has been observed that the leadership style of the managers or supervisors can significantly influence employee well-being by affecting the work culture, motivation, and overall emotional climate of the employees within the organisation. This narrative review aims to investigate how various leadership styles, specifically Transformational, Authentic, Servant, and Task-oriented leadership, impact the well-being of employees through mediating and moderating variables.
Method: Narrative review has been utilised to parse the relevant literature comprehensively, comprising both empirical and theoretical studies from PsycINFO, PubMed, and Google Scholar. The keyword used to find the studies includes “leadership style,” “transformational,” “authentic,” “servant,” and “employee well-being.” For review purposes, 20 peer-reviewed studies were selected that met the set criteria for inclusion while opinion papers and non-empirical works were excluded. Both cross-sectional and longitudinal studies were analysed to ensure comprehensive coverage.
Results: From the review, it has been found that transformational and authentic leadership show positive associations with employee well-being by means of various mediator variables like meaningful work, trust, and empowerment. On the other hand, servant leadership enhances psychological well-being and job satisfaction by keeping in priority the employees’ growth. Task-oriented leadership supports eudaimonic well-being by focusing on the structure and purpose of work. It has also been noted that various moderator variables, such as cultural context, psychological safety, and job stressors significantly shape the association between the variables.
Implications: From the review findings, the priority needs to be placed on developing leadership programs that emphasise authenticity

title: How Ozempic is Changing Dating:  GLP-1 Weight Loss Medications Are Reshaping Body Confidence, Desire, and Stigma
description:
Background
Recent increases in the use of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1s) have generated widespread public interest in their physical and psychological effects, yet little research has examined how these medications may shape romantic and sexual experiences.

Aim
The present study investigated associations between GLP-1 use for weight loss and dating outcomes, sexual experiences, and perceived stigma among single adults in the United States.

Methods
Participants were 2,002 demographically representative single adults residing in the United States who completed measures assessing GLP-1 use, perceived changes in dating and sexual experiences, and concerns about judgment related to medication use.

Outcomes
Primary outcomes included perceived changes in dating experiences, sexual experiences, confidence, sexual functioning, and stigma associated with GLP-1 use.

Results
Overall, 7.7% of participants reported using GLP-1 medications for weight loss in the past year. Among users, approximately one-third reported improvements in their dating lives and sex lives, although substantial variability emerged across outcomes. Some participants reported increased confidence, greater dating engagement, improved sexual functioning, and enhanced body comfort, whereas others reported reduced dating interest, lower confidence, or worsened sexual experiences. Gender differences also emerged. Men were more likely than women to report increases in dating confidence, changes in dating behavior, improvements in sexual functioning, and greater concern about being judged for using GLP-1 medications. Women were more likely to report no changes in sexual outcomes and lower concern about stigma.

title: Cooperation increases verbal and spatial coordination in human foraging groups in the wild
description: The diversity of foraging styles across environments and social systems is a key driver of the success of our species. Yet the human foraging literature is largely observational, since experimental manipulations in situ are difficult. We investigated highly experienced foragers (ice fishers) in situ through direct experimental manipulations: Foragers fished alone or in groups, and participants in groups were incentivised to either compete or cooperate. High-precision GPS tracking and head-camera data recording foraging behaviour, catch success, and verbal communication, combined with cognitive-computational modelling, showed that foragers adaptively integrated socioecological information. Across all conditions, foragers travelled further when unsuccessful; in groups, they also considered the locations of group members when deciding where to go. Cooperative foragers communicated more, and approached others more frequently, but did not outperform competitive foragers. Our study highlights the adaptive nature of human foraging behaviour, demonstrating how group setting and incentive structures shape spatial decision-making and communication strategies.

title: Social information use across the lifespan
description: Social information shapes how humans learn, decide, and coordinate. Theory predicts that social information is most valuable early in life, but how social information use changes across the lifespan remains poorly understood. Across seven belief-updating experiments with museum samples from Germany and Japan (ages 6–99 years; N = 41,015), we find a robust age-related trajectory: Social information use is highest early in life, drops sharply until late adolescence, and then rises slowly into late adulthood. Participants at all ages used social information most when it was close to their own belief, supported by convergent social inputs, and came from young adults. Female participants used slightly more social information than male participants, and participants from Germany used more social information than those from Japan. Together, these results reveal early-emerging strategic social information use and help explain information flow in age-diverse populations.

title: A phylogenetically conserved microstructural primitive of goal-directed action in humans and macaques
description: The capacity to override well-learned automaticity in the service of explicit goals is foundational to flexible cognition, yet whether the dual-process architecture supporting context-dependent goal-directedness is a deep cognitive primitive or a contingent product of human culture, language, and instruction has remained untested. Recent work in humans suggests that operant responding is not a uniform stream but unfolds in short bursts of rapid actions separated by longer pauses, and that these bursts decompose into two behaviourally and computationally distinct components: within-burst responses, the rapid actions that sustain an already-ongoing burst (for example, the second, third, and subsequent presses in a quick run of presses), which carry an outcome-sensitive, goal-directed signature; and burst-initiation responses, the first action that breaks a pause and starts a new burst, which operates closer to a motivationally cached, model-free regime. The long-standing random-ratio versus random-interval (RR vs RI) difference in goal-directedness reflects a schedule-driven shift in the composition of these two components rather than a difference at the schedule level. Here we provide the first phylogenetic test of this microstructural primitive by directly comparing rhesus macaques (n = 3) and human adults (n = 60) on matched RR and yoked-RI schedules. IRT distributions in both species were well described by a common bi-exponential mixture, and Welch two one-sided tests against an a-priori ±1 SD(humans) bound established statistical equivalence on all three mixture parameters (λ_fast, λ_slow, p) under both schedules. Both species exhibited the same RR-driven elevation of the within-burst proportion, and the cross-species microstructural match was present from the earliest assessable macaque training stage and remained stable across mid- and late-training blocks. title: Limes Master Edition: Using Behavioural Data to Refine Game Mechanics in Research
description: Educational video games are increasingly used in experimental research to examine their effects on learning and motivation. However, many studies focus primarily on outcome measures such as pre–post knowledge tests or self-reported engagement, while paying limited attention to behavioural data generated during gameplay. As a result, it often remains unclear which specific game features contribute to learning outcomes. This paper argues that behavioural logging within educational games can play an important methodological role in experimental research by revealing how learners interact with key game mechanics and by informing the iterative refinement of these mechanics. I illustrate this argument using Limes, a Unity-based educational video game designed to teach Roman history, as a methodological case study based on previously conducted research. The paper draws on findings from two previously conducted experimental studies investigating different aspects of the game design. In these studies, behavioural logs captured players’ interactions with several gameplay features, including optional Codex entries that provided additional historical information. Analyses indicated that engagement with Codex content was positively associated with knowledge acquisition, highlighting the Codex system as a learning-relevant feature within the game environment. Based on these insights, the Codex system was iteratively redesigned during the continued development of the game, leading to a revised version (Limes Master Edition) with more precise behavioural tracking. While earlier versions tracked Codex engagement at a general level, the revised version implemented a logging architecture capable of recording interactions with individual Codex entries. This modification enables future research to analyse detailed patterns of information-seeking behaviour and to better understand how optional learning resources are used during gameplay. title: Audio features impact the semantic content of music-evoked thoughts
description: Music permeates our everyday environments and can elicit a wide range of thoughts for the listener. To understand the mechanisms through which music steers ongoing thoughts, previous studies have investigated the effects of different music genres or excerpts on the content of music-evoked thoughts. However, 'genre' is a very broad and potentially ambiguous category (e.g., “pop music”) and 'excerpt' is too narrow to allow generalization of results. The current study explored how music shapes thoughts with a mid-level approach based on features derived from the audio. We collected open-text descriptions of music-evoked thoughts from approximately 1800 participants and extracted 27 audio features across seven acoustic domains from our music stimuli (120 instrumental excerpts from a range of genres). By applying natural language processing methods to the open-text data, we measured the general semantic similarity for the thoughts (via word2vec) and decomposed thought contents into 16 semantic topics (via Latent Dirichlet Allocation). Then we used regression models to map the audio profile of the music to the semantic profile of the thoughts. We found that the audio features effectively explained both variance in the general structure of the semantic similarity space and in the topic-specific contents of the thoughts. Our results demonstrate that auditory features serve as a window into how music impacts ongoing thoughts, providing a key method for future targeted investigations of how music can be used in everyday and clinical settings to shape listeners’ mental experience.

title: Relationship between personal responsibility to reduce climate change and trust in politics: a brief multi-level analysis using data from 28 countries
description: This study examines how trust in various political institutions and satisfaction with democratic processes are related with individuals' perceived personal responsibility to reduce climate change. European Social Survey (ESS), Round 11 data, involving participants from 28 European countries (N = 35,867) was used for the analysis. Multilevel modelling was applied to test whether trust and satisfaction with government institutions predicted personal responsibility to reduce climate change. Results revealed that trust in a country’s parliament, trust in the European Parliament, trust in the United Nations, and satisfaction with the way democracy works in the country predict higher personal responsibility to reduce climate change, while satisfaction with the national government predicts lower personal responsibility.

title: Analyzing Perceptions of Custodial Torture Among Police Officers and the Public in India
description:
This study investigates the perceptions of custodial torture among the public and the police in North India. It aims to bridge a significant gap in literature by exploring the social perception of the ongoing widespread practice of custodial torture in India, despite laws that ban the practice. We set out to examine whether public perception (n = 34) broadly endorsed or condemned custodial violence, compared to the police (n = 15), using questions adapted from the literature on custodial torture and police brutality. Our results reveal concurrence between the police and the public on the acceptability of custodial violence, alongside an awareness of its illegality. However, the views of the police differ from the public on the practice of custodial violence: police predominantly disagree with statements that claim widespread use of custodial violence, or that condemn such violence, while the public predominantly agree with such statements. This study contributes to the limited literature on custodial torture; future research can build on this study, exploring other aspects of public perception that enable torture by incorporating wider sets of questions and techniques to capture a better understanding of the phenomenon.
Keywords: custodial torture, perceptions, public, police officers, India

title: Gendered Motives for Group Formidability Among Children and Adults
description: Recent decades have seen a surge of research revealing the core, early-emerging psychological building-blocks for navigating human societies. Yet, how such core motives operate across life, undergirding political ideology, remains unknown. Here we use the same kind of minimal, abstract group stimuli across the lifespan to show that gendered preferences for majority groups manifest among preschoolers and adults alike (but not among preverbal infants) and that they motivate support for sustaining intergroup hierarchies (e.g., ethnic persecution, militarism, and social welfare opposition) among adults. Preschool (N = 317) boys, but not girls, preferred majority rather than minority members, whereas infants (N = 180) chose randomly between the two. Among adults (N = 3467), males also liked the majority more than females and these coalitional preferences correlated robustly with political ideology. These results indicate that gendered motives for intergroup formidability are rooted in earliest childhood once children begin navigating peer relationships independently.

title: Cultural models of emotion manifest in descriptions of everyday experience: A case study of the US and Belgium
description: Language provides a window onto how people conceptualize their subjective experiences, including emotions. Although rare, linguistic analyses that go beyond emotion words provide deep insights into emotional experience across cultures. In this study, we explored cultural models of emotions prevalent in the US and Belgium using verbal descriptions of recent emotional events collected from speakers of North American (US) English and Belgian Dutch in form of semi-structured interviews. We analyzed the interviews in three stages: 1) topic modeling to characterize content, 2) word counting to examine linguistic resources, and 3) inductive analysis to uncover broader themes. Our findings revealed notable cultural differences alongside some similarities. US English speakers used more first-person pronouns and emotion words, emphasized high-arousal emotions, and prioritized asserting personal achievements and openly expressing their feelings. In contrast, Belgian Dutch speakers’ descriptions reflected a more moderated approach to emotions, illustrating how social standards and broader worldviews gave meaning to the events, with use of fewer first-person pronouns and more language focused on relativization and comparison. Taken together, our observations are consistent with previous psychological research on US and Belgian culture. We evaluate our approach against other means of exploring the conceptualization of emotion across cultures.

title: Resilience in Times of Transition: A Qualitative Study of Autistic Higher Education Students During the Return to In-Person Learning.
description:
This qualitative study explored factors affecting resilience among higher education (HE) students on the autism spectrum during the significant transition to in-person classes following the COVID-19 lockdown. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with nine participants aged 20 to 36 years, all with formal diagnoses of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) attending colleges and universities across the United Kingdom. Data were analysed using inductive thematic analysis.
The analysis identified six main factors influencing resilience, organised into three enablers and three barriers. Enablers of resilience included: (1) support systems encompassing family, institutional, and mental health professional support; (2) coping strategies such as structured planning and music-based techniques, alongside personal attributes including determination and perseverance; and (3) adaptation to social distancing measures, which paradoxically facilitated resilience for some autistic students. Barriers to resilience comprised: (1) mental well-being struggles, particularly fear of infection, general anxiety, and social anxiety; (2) negative perceptions regarding the importance of in-person learning, with participants preferring remote modalities; and (3) sensory challenges.
The study demonstrates that resilience is a complex process shaped by interactions between individual characteristics and environmental factors. These findings contribute to limited existing research on resilience in autistic higher education students and highlight the need for targeted support during transitions. Insights from this research can inform the development of campus-based interventions—such as dedicated sensory spaces and flexible learning options—and guide institutional practices aimed at enhancing resilience, well-being, and academic success among autistic students during periods of significant change and uncertainty.

title: More doubt and disorderly: Revisiting the causal relationship between conspiracy beliefs and ambivalence
description: The link between conspiracy beliefs and political extremism suggests that these beliefs may contribute to attitude polarisation. However, the interplay between attitudinal processes and conspiracy beliefs have been understudied—particularly in the context of ambivalent attitudes. Across three pre-registered experiments, we examined the causal relationship between conspiracy beliefs and attitudinal ambivalence. We did not replicate prior findings suggesting that induced ambivalence would motivate greater reliance on conspiracy beliefs as a compensatory mechanism to cope with attitude conflict (Study 1). Furthermore, we unexpectedly found that conspiracy beliefs were positively associated with ambivalence (Study 2), and that exposure to conspiracy theories increased ambivalence (Study 3). These results suggest that conspiracy theories may intensify, rather than alleviate, attitude conflict and the discomfort associated with it. This research contributes to the comprehension of the attitudinal consequences of conspiracy beliefs, highlighting their potential to hinder people’s evaluative judgement.

title: Road Crossing Challenges in Autistic Adolescents: A Caregiver‑Reported Survey
description: Anecdotal evidence shows parents’ concern about autistic adolescents’ road-crossing safety, yet little evidence describes the specific challenges involved, contexts in which they occur, and how they relate to individual characteristics. To address this gap, caregivers of autistic adolescents aged 10–18 years (N = 151) completed a questionnaire assessing individual characteristics, road-crossing challenges, context-specific items, AQ-Adolescent, and coping strategies. Principal components analysis identified three road-crossing challenge dimensions: Core Road-Crossing Competency, Anxiety and Avoidance, and Use of Road Infrastructure Competency, with the first two reported more frequent difficulties. Two context-specific dimensions emerged: Physical Contexts and Psychological & Social Contexts, with the latter rated as more challenging. Regression analyses indicated that higher support needs predicted greater difficulties across all challenge and context dimensions, while co-occurring conditions, and AQ-social skills scores predicted specific dimensions only. Findings suggest that autistic adolescents’ road-crossing difficulties are multidimensional and vary by individual profile, supporting targeted guidance for families and practitioners.

title: Unconscious processing of naturalistic scenes revealed by eye movement dynamics
description: The scope of unconscious processing is continuously debated. Here, we focus on scene processing without awareness: During conscious scene processing, the eyes are attracted to meaningful and visually salient areas, yet it is unknown if this occurs for unconscious processing. In two preregistered experiments, fifty-two participants were instructed to freely view scenes presented consciously or unconsciously with Continuous Flash Suppression stimulation. For invisible scenes, participants gazed more, but not longer, on objects and emotional faces, and were attracted to areas that are both semantically and visually salient. However, a comparison of eye movements with a Convolutional Neural Network mimicking the human visual ventral pathway revealed that unconscious gaze patterns correlated only with layers corresponding with early visual processes, while conscious patterns correlated also with higher-level layers. This suggests that even without awareness, the eyes are attracted to meaningful areas in scenes, though such processing is limited compared to conscious viewing.

title: Prospects for AI-driven interpretation of real-world pupil dynamics: Moving toward natural neuroscience
description: Measuring human brain activity in the real world has long remained a major challenge in conventional neuroscience. Pupil dynamics offer a promising non-invasive proxy for arousal-related multidimensional brain states. However, interpreting pupil data collected outside the laboratory is notoriously difficult due to complex, multilayered factors, including lighting conditions, arousal states, cognitive control as well as the influence of the viscoelastic properties of the iris, that can confound results. Here, we propose an AI-driven analytical strategy as a potential solution to this interpretational bottleneck. We discuss an approach that combines deep learning with mechanical physics equations to predict and model human pupil dynamics from multimodal contexts, such as first-person vision video and physiological and physical data as well as the application of translational data from non-human studies. This AI strategy, combined with consideration of the viscoelastic properties of the iris, may enable the extraction of internal-state (i.e., neurological) factors by detangling complex real-world pupil data. It may, in addition, lead to the development of virtual predictions of internal states even in the absence of pupil data. While there are challenges to realizing this vision, this approach has great potential to contribute to NeuroAI as it could open a promising new door to natural neuroscience in fields such as sports science, clinical medicine, and human-computer interaction.

title: Modeling Decision Bias in dockerHDDM: A Systematic Comparison and Evaluation
description: Decision bias refers to a systematic tendency to approach or avoid a particular option in two-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) tasks. With the advent of easy-to-use tools, diffusion-decision model (DDM) is widely used to distinguish two types of latent cognitive processes, bias in starting point or in efficiency, providing a powerful tool for understanding a variety of psychological phenomena across different fields. However, correctly estimating these two types of bias requires specifying the model to match the type of bias being investigated. So far, no study has systematically evaluated the different model configurations for modelling decision bias in HDDM, the most widely used python package for DDM. Here we evaluated nine model specifications using the three main modeling modules in HDDM across both simulated and empirical data. Our results show that the default function, which uses accuracy coding of data without flipping parameters, fails to recover either the starting point bias or the drift rate bias. Only model specifications that directly estimate the drift bias parameter, drift criterion (dc), or apply appropriate parameter flipping recover true bias parameters. By applying optimal specification to empirical data, we uncovered a novel psychological effect that went undetected in the original study. We provide concrete, evidence based recommendations for model specification and fully reproducible code. This work ensures accurate parameter estimation and the correct interpretation of parameter when modeling decision biases.

title: Rubric-Guided Generative AI for Scalable Creativity Assessment in Educational Games
description: Assessing creativity at scale remains challenging in learning sciences. This study examined whether GPT-4o could assess creativity in 421 student-designed levels from Physics Playground. Using a structured rubric, GPT-4o ratings were compared with human raters. Results showed strong correlations (r = .74) with multimodal inputs, and reliability analyses showed consistent performance across runs. Findings suggest that rubric-guided LLMs can approximate human creativity judgments efficiently. This approach offers a promising method for scalable automated creativity assessment.

title: Generative AI for Creative Learning in K-12 Education: Insights from a Systematic Scoping Review
description: The rapid rise of generative AI (GenAI) presents both opportunities and challenges for fostering creativity in K–12 education. This systematic scoping review synthesized 45 studies (2017–2025) to examine how GenAI has been applied in creative learning. Four categories emerged: (1) creativity assessment, (2) human–AI co-creativity, (3) stakeholders’ perceptions, and (4) creativity enhancement. Findings show strong potential for GenAI to support idea generation, multimodal expression, and assessment of creative outputs, but highlight concerns about equity, authorship, and theoretical grounding. While most applications focus on text-based creativity, multimodal and culturally inclusive approaches remain underexplored. This review provides a foundation for responsible and equitable integration of GenAI into K–12 classrooms and captures a field in transition, where new forms of creative expression are emerging and educators are rethinking assessment, authorship, and pedagogy. This review provides a foundation for ethically grounded, developmentally appropriate and theory-driven GenAI designs that enhance, rather than automate, human creativity.

title: Cumulative link models — CLM & CLMM (para análise de variáveis dependentes ordinais)
description: Este tutorial apresenta os modelos de regressão ordinal da família Cumulative Link Model (CLM) e Cumulative Link Mixed Model (CLMM), implementados no pacote ordinal (Christensen, 2019) para o R. O foco é prático e voltado a pesquisadores em linguística e áreas afins que trabalham com variáveis dependentes em escala ordinal, como julgamentos de aceitabilidade, avaliações de sotaque ou escalas de atitude. O tutorial cobre: (1) visualização de dados ordinais com o pacote likert (Bryer; Speerschneider, 2025); (2) a lógica dos modelos cumulativos, incluindo probabilidades cumulativas, função de ligação e variável latente; (3) ajuste e interpretação do clm para observações independentes; (4) ajuste e interpretação do clmm com efeitos aleatórios para dados com medidas repetidas; (5) verificação do pressuposto de proporcionalidade das odds; (6) probabilidades preditas e visualização dos efeitos do modelo; (7) comparação de modelos via AIC e Likelihood Ratio Test; e (8) um modelo de reporte para artigos científicos. Não é exigido conhecimento prévio de regressão ordinal, mas familiaridade básica com R e com os conceitos de regressão linear ou logística é recomendada.

title: Climate change and conflict: The vicious cycles undermining climate action, and what can be done to break them
description: In this review, we synthesise evidence to argue that climate change and conflict are mutually reinforcing. We first examine conflict as a barrier to mitigation, focusing on four faultlines that slow climate action: (a) ideological polarisation, (b) vertical “elite versus ordinary people” narratives, (c) intranational, place-based conflicts, and (d) international disputes. The consequence of these conflicts is worsening climate change, which in turn increases the prevalence of factors known to be conflict amplifiers: heat stress; resource scarcity and economic stress; widening inequality; and forced displacement. Our analysis points to the potential for recursive “climate–conflict loops”, fuelled in part by erosion of institutional trust, shrinking moral circles, political polarisation, and de-prioritisation of long-term climate goals. In a spirit of optimism, however, we identify three buffers capable of breaking these vicious cycles: maintenance of procedural and distributive justice; enhancing information integrity; and scaffolding institutional cooperation. We conclude by proposing a research agenda that integrates psychological mechanisms into dynamic, multi-level accounts of how climate impacts and political conflict coevolve.

title: Age and Lifelong Cognitive Stimulation Shape the Representational Basis of Learning
description: Configurations often predict outcomes that differ from those predicted by their individual elements, posing a fundamental challenge for learning. In complex environments, learners must balance competing computational priorities: whereas configural learning supports specific, context-sensitive associations at the expense of reduced generalization, elemental learning enables efficient generalization across experiences but is less effective at learning configural relationships. How aging and lifelong cognitive enrichment influence the representations deployed during learning remains unclear. Using a task that dissociates configural from elemental learning, we show that older adults rely less on configural learning and more on elemental learning relative to younger adults, indicating greater reliance on representations that generalize value across related stimuli, even when maladaptive for the task. Furthermore, higher lifelong cognitive stimulation was associated with greater reliance on elemental relative to configural learning. Together, these findings suggest that both aging and lifelong engagement in cognitively enriching activities influence how people balance the competing priorities of specificity and generalization during learning.

title: From the Inside Out: School Stressors Identified by Autistic and ADHD (AuDHD) Students Experiencing School Non-Attendance
description:
Research into school non-attendance is expanding, yet the perspectives of young people, particularly neurodivergent students, remain underrepresented. Card-sorting tasks offer a promising, accessible method for capturing these perspectives. The Student Stress Investigation (SSI) uses a structured card-sort approach to facilitate young people’s self-report of school-related stressors.

This study used the SSI to explore school-based stressors among 31 children and adolescents (mean age = 12.16 years) diagnosed with both autism and ADHD (AuDHD). On average, they missed 3.46 days of school per month. Participants first categorised stressors as relevant or irrelevant, then ranked relevant items from smallest to largest stressors.

The most frequently identified major stressors were classroom environments that were too loud or quiet (35.5%), uninteresting tasks (32.2%), unpredictability (29.0%), school days being too long (29.0%), and being rushed (29.0%). Qualitative responses highlighted variability in how stressors were experienced. For example, some students reported that the classroom being too loud or quiet was a sensory-related stressor, while others reported it as having an impact on attention or executive functioning.

These findings provide direct insight into the everyday school experiences contributing to stress and non-attendance among AuDHD students. The results underscore the value of self-report tools and highlight the need for targeted, individualised, and proactive adjustments to reduce stress that may in turn support an increased capacity to consider a return to school.

title: The WEIRD instrument problem and systematic bias
description: As researchers broaden studies to populations that are not Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic (WEIRD), they typically use instruments originally developed for WEIRD populations. This paper formalizes the resulting "WEIRD instrument problem," whereby WEIRD instruments systematically bias cross-cultural research. For example, small-scale and non-Western populations are commonly found to have less complex personality structures than WEIRD societies, a finding often attributed to non-WEIRD psychologies or societies being less complex. However, using simulation models, I demonstrate that instruments designed for one reference (WEIRD) population systematically underestimate the complexity of novel populations, even if the underlying psychologies or societies are equally complex. The degree of underestimation closely tracks cultural dissimilarity from the reference society, rather than actual differences in complexity. Empirically supporting this theoretical prediction, I find that cultural distance from the United States, the WEIRD reference society for which a cross-cultural personality instrument was designed, has the strongest negative relationship with personality structure complexity, as measured by that instrument, across a dataset of 67 countries. This strongly supports the hypothesis that lower apparent complexity outside WEIRD populations results from the use of WEIRD instruments, rather than from real differences in complexity. Beyond cross-cultural research, similar logic applies whenever an instrument designed for one group, such as one gender, one cohort, or one species, is administered more broadly. Addressing this problem requires cautious interpretation of cross-population research, designing cross-population instruments from the ground up, and, ultimately, building better theories of causation and measurement in the behavioral sciences.

title: The Impact of Unconditional Prenatal and Infant Cash Transfers on Maternal Anxiety
description:
Background: Maternal mental health is associated with maternal, infant, and family outcomes. Economic hardship during the perinatal period increases the risk of adverse maternal mental health outcomes, including clinically significant maternal anxiety. 
Objectives: This study examined the association between exposure to the Rx Kids program, a universal and unconditional prenatal and infant cash transfer program in Flint, Michigan, and maternal anxiety in a sample of mothers residing in Flint and surrounding communities (N=1,197). 
Design: Utilizing a cross-sectional design and controlling for covariates, we analyzed anxiety ratings among mothers exposed to Rx Kids and mothers in three non-exposed temporal and geographic comparison groups. 
Methods: A multivariable difference-in-differences model assessed associations between maternal anxiety, program exposure, geographic location (i.e., within or outside the program implementation community), and time (i.e., during or before program implementation). 
Results: In comparison to Flint mothers prior to Rx Kids, exposed mothers reported significantly less moderate to severe anxiety (-9.5 percentage points, p < .05), lower mean GAD-7 scores (-1.5 percentage points, p < .05), and significantly decreased frequency of nervousness (-13.5 percentage points, p < .01) and worrying too much (-9.8 percentage points, p < .05). Relative to all geographic and temporal comparison groups, mothers exposed to Rx Kids were less likely to report clinically elevated anxiety (-10 percentage points, p < .10); they were also less likely to report frequently experiencing nervousness (-10 percentage points, p < .10) and fear (-10 percentage points, p < .05). 
Conclusion: Exposure to universal, unconditional prenatal and infant cash transfers was associated with lower maternal anxiety and less frequent core anxiety symptoms in the postpartum period. Given that upstream economic interventions may improve maternal mental health

title: MASEMiner – AI-Assisted Data Extraction  for Meta-Analytic Structural Equation Modeling
description: Meta-analytic structural equation modeling (MASEM) synthesizes multivariate evidence across studies, allowing researchers to examine theory-driven path models, including mediated and predictive effects, and to evaluate the dimensional structure of psychological and behavioral measures. A major bottleneck is the labor-intensive extraction of statistical information from primary studies. Large language models and vision-language models offer new opportunities for extracting such heterogeneous statistics from textual and visual document content. Building on these capabilities, we introduce MASEMiner, an open-source application for AI-assisted extraction and verification of data required for MASEM that can be run locally or accessed through a hosted web interface. MASEMiner supports the extraction of directly reported correlations and related effect sizes as well as indirect information (i.e., factor loadings and factor correlations) used to reconstruct correlation matrices for MASEM. We evaluated MASEMiner’s extraction accuracy across four use cases covering directly and indirectly reported statistics. Outputs were compared with human consensus codings from published meta-analytic databases, using separate study sets for prompt development and evaluation. Precision was near-perfect for indirectly reported information (0.95–1.00) but lower for some directly reported quantities such as effect sizes (~0.65), where the tool over-extracted candidate values. Recovery was high, with sensitivity above 0.90 for almost all extracted variables. MASEMiner supports a human-in-the-loop workflow by extracting candidate statistics that can be efficiently checked against the source documents, thereby reducing manual coding effort while preserving transparency and reproducibility in research synthesis.

title: A Unified Framework for Psychometrics in Experimental Psychology: The Standardized Generalized Hierarchical Factor Model
description: To address Cronbach’s longstanding call to unify experimental and correlational psychology, Hierarchical Factor Models (HFMs) have emerged as a promising approach to estimate individual differences while accounting for trial-level noise. As formalized by Rouder et al. (2025), this framework assumes Gaussian response times (RTs) and operates in raw units. Here, we generalize this framework by introducing the Standardized Generalized HFM (GenHFM), which incorporates two natural extensions: explicitly modeling asymmetric distributions and implementing a fully standardized latent structure. First, modeling asymmetry allows us to capture the true shape of RTs and, crucially, quantify the bias introduced by fitting Gaussian HFMs to skewed data. Second, the standardized parameterization ensures transparent prior specification and facilitates the analysis of factor loadings, enabling researchers to directly compare the degree of association between experimental effects and common factors, regardless of their original metrics. Consequently, this allows researchers to evaluate the discriminative capacity of each task regarding the latent process, mirroring the assessment of construct validity in classical psychometrics within experimental settings. We conducted a simulation study showing that Gaussian HFMs can underestimate true correlations by up to 50%, whereas GenHFM yields unbiased and more efficient estimates. Finally, we re-analyze data from two published studies using executive control tasks to illustrate the empirical application of these models. Furthermore, we show that GenHFM achieves better predictive accuracy than alternative models typically used in the field.

title: Allocating Commitment Under Uncertainty: A Formal Theory of Intention Formation
description:
Humans regularly form intentions to guide future behaviour; yet many intentions fail to translate into effective goal pursuit. Forming implementation intentions—or context-specific if–then plans—can improve goal pursuit relative to more general goal intentions. However, current theoretical accounts of intention formation are largely descriptive and do not formally specify the conditions under which different intention strategies succeed or fail.
We introduce a formal framework conceptualising intention formation as the allocation of behavioural commitment under uncertainty. Here, an intention’s effectiveness depends on three interacting components: (1) subjective value of the goal, (2) context specificity, and (3) commitment precision—or how selectively commitment is enforced by reducing non-focal execution. This selectivity enables an efficiency–flexibility trade-off and induces costs when multiple intentions compete or when planned cues fail to materialise.
We fit the model to four established paradigms manipulating cue reliability, number of intentions, response competition, and outcome revaluation. Empirical fits shows that our model accounts for both the benefits and failures of implementation intentions that are not explained by competing accounts. This includes capturing non monotonic effects of context specificity, value by specificity interactions, multi goal reversals, and generalised reductions in behavioural flexibility.
Together, our findings identify commitment precision as a core control process in intention formation, while providing a unified account of the flexibility–efficiency trade offs that govern self regulation under uncertainty. By integrating social–personality theory with computational principles of decision making, this work advances a formal science of intention formation.

title: Youth Participatory Action Research Across Educational Contexts: A Case Study Bridging High School and University Classrooms
description: Adolescents’ health and well-being are influenced by their broader physical and social environments, yet they often lack the power and resources to create change. Youth participatory action research (YPAR) is a promising framework to support adolescents to explore issues relevant to their lives and take action to address them, while also supporting positive youth development by fulfilling key developmental needs. YPAR is increasingly implemented in schools in collaboration with university researchers, yet such collaborations are rarely embedded within university courses that can provide training in YPAR methods to university students. To address this gap, we introduce a novel “classroom-to-classroom” model of YPAR that brings together university and secondary school classrooms to engage in mutual learning and joint action and integrates strengths of traditional models of school-based YPAR and critical service learning. We illustrate how this model can be applied through a case study of our collaboration between a graduate seminar and high school classroom to investigate how pressing issues such as mental health, gun violence, and social needs (e.g., housing, green spaces) impact local youth. We discuss the unique opportunities and challenges this model presents, with a particular focus on the role of relationships and resources. We reflect on how we navigated these challenges and offer practical recommendations for university researchers and teachers seeking to promote positive youth development through YPAR across educational contexts.

title: A road map for assessing process independence in behavioral measures of attitudes: An SFT and GRT modeling analysis
description: The study of biases has long relied on behavioral measures such as the Implicit Association Test to assess the strength of links between social categories and positive or negative valence. Despite the prevalence of these measures, the perceptual mechanisms responsible for observed effects remain elusive, as the cognitive architecture that produces bias has not been formally tested. The present study applies mathematical tools from perceptual science and information-processing theory, including General Recognition Theory (GRT), mean response time invariance (mRTi), and Systems Factorial Technology (SFT), to evaluate the extent to which the processing of age and valence are independent across three different levels of processing. We used a within-subjects design combining a stimulus identification task and a categorization task to assess perceptual independence, selective-attention independence, and architectural (capacity) independence at the individual level for 97 participants. Perceptual and selective-attention independence held for the majority of participants, suggesting that early-stage processing explains a limited amount of bias. However, architectural independence failed for nearly 90% of participants, indicating that structural interactions exist during the joint processing of age and valence that affect overall processing speed. Cross-method independence profiles revealed that only a small subset of participants showed no evidence of bias across tests, indicating that age and valence may be difficult to separate at even a basic perceptual level. These results demonstrate how formal modeling tools from perceptual science can provide structural validation for implicit measures of attitudes and offer a more precise and mechanistic foundation for an interdisciplinary science of social bias.

title: Selective Exposure to Environmental Messages: Dual Sentiment Pathways to Information-Seeking Intentions
description: Environmental problems are intensifying, prompting expanded public communication efforts to raise awareness and motivate pro-environmental behavior. However, meaningful engagement with environmental messages is often selective, as people actively choose among many competing messages. In this paper, we examined how active engagement with environmental messages shapes enduring affective orientations (i.e., sentiments) towards environmental issues. Using a selective exposure paradigm, we exposed participants to four types of environmental messages varying in valence (positive vs. negative) and personal relevance (human vs. animal). We proposed that engagement with these messages would shape hopeful and anxious sentiments toward environmental issues. These sentiment shifts, in turn, were expected to predict the likelihood of participants seeking further environmental information. In an initial exploratory study (N = 283), participants’ selection of the different kinds of environmental messages showed no direct effect on environmental information-seeking intentions. Further analyses revealed two competing indirect paths: (a) increased seeking intentions via enhanced anxious sentiments and (b) reduced seeking intentions via diminished hopeful sentiments. These patterns were replicated in a confirmatory study (N = 1,009), demonstrating their robustness. Together, these findings suggest that the effectiveness of environmental communication is not limited to valence-congruent sentiments. Instead, the balance of emotional reactions that messages trigger shapes information-seeking behavior.

title: Trustworthiness Perception in the Absence of Any Persons
description: People rely on their perception of a person’s trustworthiness to make important social decisions. Consequently, the misperception of trustworthiness may lead to undesirable outcomes. Trustworthiness perception has been widely studied with unnatural and static faces, however, people must also consider contextual information when making social inferences. In this study, we investigated the importance of context in trustworthiness judgments by having 124 observers continuously rate the perceived trustworthiness of a blurred-out (invisible) target character in 12 videos. We found that contextual and facial cues contribute similar amounts of information to trustworthiness judgments (~20% variance explained), however, observers can better infer others’ trustworthiness (t(80) = -3.40, p = 0.001) and agree more with each other (t(80) = -592.56, p < 0.001) when using contextual information than face and body information. Our findings highlight the importance of using contextual information when inferring the trustworthiness of others.
